common_name: Spirit of the Holy Ghost Philodendron (Spiritus-Sancti Philodendron)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in warm, humid conditions and grow on a moss pole or against a bark slab; this is a slow, hemi-epiphytic climber that needs high humidity and consistent warmth above 65°F to establish.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light with a rough support surface for the aerial roots to grip, keeping humidity high and never letting the chunky aroid mix go fully dry. Philodendron spiritus-sancti is a critically endangered hemi-epiphytic climber known from only a handful of wild plants on a granite outcrop in Espírito Santo, Brazil, which has made it one of the most sought-after and expensive philodendrons in cultivation. Its leaves are long, narrow, and strap-like with an undulating margin rather than the broad heart shape typical of most collector philodendrons, and juvenile foliage carries a distinctive silvery cast that fades toward matte olive-green as the leaf matures and the pale midrib and secondary veins become more pronounced. Growth is notably slower than most climbing philodendrons in the dataset, so patience and stable warm, humid conditions matter more than fertilizer for this species. All parts toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Divide offsets or root a rooted cutting in a chunky, fast-draining aroid mix; Philodendron luxurians is a self-heading species that forms a low rosette and does best in a wide, shallow pot rather than a tall climbing setup.

directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade in a well-aerated mix, letting the surface dry slightly between waterings. Philodendron luxurians is a self-heading species from the Chocó region of Colombia and Panama that produces elongated, narrow, spear-shaped leaves with a deeply quilted, ribbed surface texture running between the lateral veins, giving each leaf a rippled, almost corrugated appearance quite different from the broad velvet or heart-shaped leaves of other philodendrons in this collection. New leaves emerge wrapped in a papery, translucent cataphyll that splits and drops away as the leaf unfurls, and the mature foliage takes on a glossy, deep forest-green with a subtly wavy margin. Unlike vining philodendrons, it stays compact and clumping, making it well suited to a shaded windowsill or protected patio container. All parts toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Set out basal offsets or divisions once night temperatures stay above 60°F, in a large container of humus-rich, well-drained soil; this self-heading species needs substantial floor or bench space as it matures.

directions: Grow in partial to deep shade with high humidity and consistently moist, never soggy, soil. Philodendron giganteum is a robust, non-climbing self-heading species native to Trinidad, the Lesser Antilles, and northern South America, distinguished from the dataset's other large-leaved philodendrons by its glossy, thick-textured, broadly heart-shaped leaves that can exceed two feet across on a mature specimen, carried on stout, upright petioles arranged in a dense rosette. The leaf surface is smoother and more lustrous than the velvety or quilted foliage of species like verrucosum or mamei, giving it a bold, waxy, almost rubbery appearance. As it matures it develops a short, thick above-ground trunk rather than climbing, making it better suited to floor-standing display than a moss pole. All parts toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Give this self-heading species ample floor or bed space and a rich, well-drained substrate; divide rooted basal shoots away from the mother plant once night temperatures stay reliably above 60°F.

directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade in a rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained mix, and give this species room to reach its full size. Philodendron speciosum is a self-heading giant from the coastal forests of Bahia and Espírito Santo, Brazil, producing some of the largest leaves of any philodendron in cultivation — elongated, arrow-shaped blades that can approach five feet in length on mature plants, with a distinctly undulating, ruffled margin unlike the flatter leaf edges of gloriosum or martianum. The petioles and new growth are flushed with deep burgundy-red, contrasting against the glossy dark green mature foliage, and this species has served as a parent of several popular self-heading hybrids in the trade. Because of its eventual scale, it is best suited to a spacious shaded garden bed or large floor container rather than a windowsill. All parts toxic if ingested.
